questions.q: In this chapter, sacredness is described as finding something that has:
questions.a: Deep religious or spiritual significance, worthy of reverence
o: Deep religious or spiritual significance, worthy of reverence
A code of conduct to be followed on a long journey
A crossing place on a river or other body of water
A relic kept as an object of reverence by its followers

questions.q: In Jainism, tirthas are mainly associated with:
questions.a: Places where Tirthankaras attained liberation or where major events of their lives occurred. Relic sites belong to Buddhism, takhts to Sikhism.
o: Places of Tirthankaras' liberation or key life events
Places where the Buddha stayed or where his relics are kept
Seats of spiritual authority linked with the Sikh Gurus
Places where the parts of a divine mother's body fell

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a Sikh takht named in the chapter?
questions.a: The Mahabodhi Stupa is a Buddhist site at Bodh Gaya. The Akal Takht and the takhts at Patna and Anandpur are the Sikh seats named.
o: Mahabodhi Stupa
Akal Takht
Takht Sri Patna Sahib
Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib

questions.q: Which site does the chapter call a relic stupa in Madhya Pradesh?
questions.a: The Great Stupa at Sanchi. The Mahabodhi Stupa at Bodh Gaya is linked to the Buddha's enlightenment, not described as the relic stupa.
o: Great Stupa at Sanchi
Mahabodhi Stupa at Bodh Gaya
Akal Takht at Amritsar
Shatrunjaya hill in Saurashtra

questions.q: Meenakshi from Madurai goes with her friend Maria to the Velankanni Church in Tamil Nadu, though Meenakshi follows a different faith. Which statement of the chapter does this illustrate?
questions.a: The chapter says followers of other faiths also visit shrines of religions that came from outside India, naming the Velankanni Church and the Dargah Sharif of Ajmer.
o: Followers of other faiths also visit shrines of outside-origin religions
Shrines of religions from outside India are meant only for their own followers
Only religions born in India can have places that are called sacred
Shrines of faiths from outside India are visited by Buddhist pilgrims only

questions.q: A Class 7 group in Patna wants one stop for the place where, according to Buddhist tradition, the Buddha attained enlightenment, and another for a relic stupa. Which plan fits the chapter?
questions.a: Bodh Gaya's Mahabodhi Stupa is where enlightenment is said to have happened, and Sanchi's Great Stupa is the relic stupa. The swapped plan reverses their roles.
o: Mahabodhi Stupa at Bodh Gaya, then the Great Stupa at Sanchi
Great Stupa at Sanchi, then the Mahabodhi Stupa at Bodh Gaya as relic stupa
Mahabodhi Stupa at Bodh Gaya, then Girnar as the relic stupa
Takht Sri Patna Sahib for enlightenment, then Sanchi for relics

questions.q:
Study the statements.
1. In this chapter, sacredness is connected only with religion and never with geography.
2. Bodh Gaya receives more than four million visitors every year.
3. Sikhs aspire to visit the takhts at least once in their lifetimes.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: the chapter links sacredness with geography and traditions as well. 2 and 3 are stated in the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Takht Sri Patna Sahib, the Akal Takht and Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib are seats of spiritual authority in Sikhism.
Reason (R): Sikh tradition records pilgrimages by Guru Nanak to places such as Haridwar, Prayag and Puri.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the Gurus' journeys to other places do not explain why the three takhts are centres of spiritual authority.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match the sacred place in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Great Stupa at Sanchi  2. Akal Takht  3. Shatrunjaya hill  4. Velankanni Church
Column B: a. Jain tirtha in Saurashtra, Gujarat  b. relic stupa in Madhya Pradesh  c. part of the Golden Temple at Amritsar  d. Tamil Nadu shrine also visited by followers of other faiths
questions.a: Sanchi is the relic stupa, the Akal Takht is part of the Golden Temple, Shatrunjaya is a Jain hill and Velankanni is the Tamil Nadu church. Each distractor swaps the descriptions of two of the four places.

questions.q: Write a three-line board that could be put up at Bodh Gaya for visitors, using three facts from the chapter.
questions.a: Any three correct facts, e.g. Mahabodhi Stupa is in Bihar; according to Buddhist tradition the Buddha attained enlightenment here; it receives more than four million visitors every year; it is an important site for pilgrims.
s: First line gives a correct fact from the chapter
Second line gives a different correct fact
Third line gives a third correct fact and nothing wrong is stated

questions.q: Compare how Buddhist and Jain sacred places are linked to great figures of the faith.
questions.a: Buddhist sites are often places the Buddha visited or where his relics are kept, such as Sanchi, or where he attained enlightenment, such as Bodh Gaya. Jain tirthas mark where Tirthankaras attained liberation or where major events of their lives occurred, such as Girnar and Shatrunjaya.
s: Buddhist link: places visited by the Buddha or holding relics, with an example
Jain link: places of liberation or major events of the Tirthankaras, with an example
Common point: both faiths tie sacred places to their great figures

questions.q: The chapter says sacredness 'is not just connected with religion and spirituality'. Name two other things with which it is connected.
questions.a: It is connected with geography and with all sorts of traditions.
s: Names geography
Names traditions

questions.q: (a) What is a relic, according to the chapter? (b) Name one relic stupa and say why a Buddhist pilgrim would value it.
questions.a: (a) A part of a saint's or spiritual figure's body, or sometimes one of their belongings, kept as an object of reverence. (b) The Great Stupa at Sanchi; Buddhist sites are often places where the Buddha's relics are kept or that he visited.
s: Part (a): relic defined as a part of the body or a belonging kept for reverence
Part (b): names Sanchi and links it to the Buddha's relics

questions.q: Name any two religions that the chapter says originated outside India, and one shrine where followers of other faiths also pray.
questions.a: Any two of Islam, Christianity, Judaism and Zoroastrianism; shrine: the Dargah Sharif of Ajmer or the Velankanni Church.
s: Two of the four outside-origin religions named
A correct shrine visited by followers of other faiths

questions.q: Differentiate between a 'shrine' and a 'pilgrimage' using the chapter's definitions.
questions.a: A shrine is a place regarded as holy because of its association with the divine, a sacred relic or a spiritual figure. A pilgrimage is a journey to a sacred place that is significant within a religion or belief system.
s: Shrine defined as a holy place
Pilgrimage defined as a journey to such a place

questions.q: (a) Name the three Sikh takhts the chapter mentions. (b) Why do Sikhs aspire to visit these places at least once in their lifetimes?
questions.a: (a) Takht Sri Patna Sahib, the Akal Takht and Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib. (b) They are associated with important Sikh Gurus and so have special significance.
s: Part (a): the three takhts named correctly
Part (b): reason that they are linked with important Gurus and hold special significance

questions.q: Anil says, 'Only religions that began in India have sacred places that people visit.' Do you agree? Support your answer with two examples from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Followers of Islam, Christianity, Judaism and Zoroastrianism, religions from outside India, have shrines where people pray, such as the Dargah Sharif of Ajmer and the Velankanni Church. The chapter adds that religions that began in India have many more sacred sites, but that does not make 'only' correct.
s: Verdict: disagrees because of the word 'only'
Two shrines of outside-origin faiths named
Notes that India-born faiths have many more sites; this does not mean only they have sacred places

questions.q: 'Almost every school of thought and religion in India has its own sacred places.' Justify this statement with examples from Buddhism, Sikhism, Jainism and the faiths that came from outside India.
questions.a: Buddhism: Sanchi and Bodh Gaya, linked to the Buddha's relics and enlightenment. Sikhism: takhts at Patna, Amritsar and Anandpur linked to the Gurus. Jainism: tirthas at Mount Abu, Girnar and Shatrunjaya where Tirthankaras attained liberation. Faiths from outside India: shrines such as the Dargah Sharif of Ajmer and the Velankanni Church. In the India-born faiths the places are usually tied to great figures.
s: Buddhist examples with what they mark
Sikh takhts with their link to the Gurus
Jain tirthas with what they mark
Shrines of faiths from outside India with an example
Concludes that sacred places are spread across faiths and tied to great figures

questions.q: Choose any two sacred places from different faiths in the chapter, for example one Buddhist and one Sikh. Show how each fits the chapter's definition of a shrine, and explain what the two choices tell you about how sacredness is connected to religion and to tradition.
questions.a: E.g. the Great Stupa at Sanchi is holy because relics are kept there; the Akal Takht is a seat of spiritual authority tied to the Gurus, whom Sikhs revere as spiritual figures. The chapter defines a shrine as a place regarded as holy because of its association with the divine, a sacred relic or a spiritual figure, and both fit. The faiths differ but each place is tied to a relic or a great figure, and the chapter adds that sacredness is connected with geography and traditions as well as with religion.
s: First place chosen and linked to a relic, the divine or a spiritual figure
Second place from a different faith chosen and linked in the same way
Chapter definition of a shrine used correctly
Notes that the faiths differ but the pattern of linking place to relic or figure is shared
Concludes that sacredness is connected with geography and traditions as well as religion

questions.q:
The 45 students of Class 7 in a Gaya school have one outing to plan. Option P is a famous stupa in Madhya Pradesh; the train and stay would cost Rs 2,700 per student. Option Q is a stupa in their own district, reached by a bus costing Rs 9,000 in all. The school fund holds Rs 1,00,000.
(a) Name P and Q, and say what kind of stupa P is.
(b) Find the total cost of each option and say whether the fund can pay for P.
(c) What does Q mark in Buddhist tradition, and what visitor figure does the chapter give for it?
(d) Which option should the school choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) P: the Great Stupa at Sanchi, a relic stupa; Q: the Mahabodhi Stupa at Bodh Gaya. (b) P: 45 x 2,700 = Rs 1,21,500, which is Rs 21,500 more than the fund; Q: Rs 9,000, well within it. (c) Q is where the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment; the chapter gives over four million visitors a year. (d) Either if reasoned: Q is affordable and is the enlightenment site visited by millions; P cannot be afforded without extra money but gives the relic stupa, so it needs a way to raise Rs 21,500.
s: Part (a): Sanchi as the relic stupa and Bodh Gaya named
Part (b): Rs 1,21,500 for P, short by Rs 21,500, and Rs 9,000 for Q
Part (c): enlightenment and over four million visitors a year
Part (d): chooses P or Q and justifies with the cost figures and a chapter fact

questions.q:
Kavya and Arjun are making a class poster. It has two columns: 'Shrines of religions that began outside India' and 'Shrines of religions that began in India'. They have these cards: Dargah Sharif of Ajmer, Girnar, Velankanni Church, Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib. There is room for only one extra card, a Buddhist site or a Jain site.
(a) Place the four cards in the correct columns.
(b) What do the Ajmer and Velankanni shrines show about who may visit them?
(c) What do Jain tirthas such as Girnar mark?
(d) Which extra card would you add, and how does it improve the poster?
questions.a: (a) Outside India: Dargah Sharif of Ajmer, Velankanni Church. In India: Girnar (Jain) and Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib (Sikh). (b) Followers of other faiths also visit them. (c) Places where Tirthankaras attained liberation or where major events of their lives occurred. (d) Either: a Buddhist card such as Sanchi or Bodh Gaya adds a third India-born faith linked to the Buddha; a second Jain card such as Mount Abu is acceptable if reasoned.
s: Part (a): all four cards placed correctly
Part (b): visited by followers of other faiths too
Part (c): Tirthankaras' liberation or major life events
Part (d): picks a card and says what it adds from the chapter

questions.q: The chapter says a tirtha literally means:
questions.a: A place where one can cross a river or other body of water; symbolically it is a crossing to a higher life.
o: A place where one can cross a river or water body
A person who guides the crossing to higher life
A hilltop shrine reached by a long trek
A group walk held regularly every year

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of the pilgrimage tradition described in the chapter?
questions.a: It did not begin with modern transport: Indians crossed the Subcontinent for at least 3,000 years with no modern means of transportation.
o: It began only after modern transport arrived
It is an inner journey as well as a physical journey
It involves a specified code of conduct to be followed
It has been continuous for at least 3,000 years

questions.q: Which figure does the chapter give for the age of the Pandharpur wari?
questions.a: The chapter calls it an 800-year-old tradition. 3,000 years is the minimum age of pilgrimage in general, 21 is the days of the walk, and 6 is the Prayagraj Kumbh interval.
o: 800 years
3,000 years
21 years
6 years

questions.q: The Sabarimala temple in Kerala is dedicated to which deity?
questions.a: Ayyappa. Vithoba is the deity at Pandharpur and Niyam Raja is the supreme deity of the Dongria Khond hill.
o: Ayyappa
Vithoba
Niyam Raja
Shiva

questions.q: About a dozen villagers reach Delhi station on the way back from Rameswaram and say they must only change trains there, as they are heading to Haridwar. What does this best show about their journey?
questions.a: They were on one long tirthayatra covering several sacred places, so Delhi was only a change of train. They carried food for themselves, not goods to sell.
o: One tirthayatra planned to cover several distant sacred places
A trading trip meant to sell atta and ghee in the Delhi market
A journey with no sacred purpose that happened to cross the whole of India
A short visit made only to cross a river on the way back home

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Indians have made pilgrimages for at least 3,000 years, even when there was no modern transport.
2. A pilgrimage, as the chapter describes it, is only a physical journey and needs no code of conduct.
3. Symbolically, a tirtha is a place where one can cross from ordinary worldly life to a higher, spiritual life.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 is false: the chapter calls pilgrimage an inner journey that requires a specified code of conduct. 1 and 3 are stated in the chapter.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: Ravi's cousin says, 'The old trek to the hilltop shrine at Sabarimala was so hard that it must have been meant to put people off.' According to the chapter, what does such a difficult approach symbolise?
questions.a: The chapter says a challenging approach, common to many hilltop shrines, symbolises the difficulties of the inner path.
o: The difficulties of the inner path
A crossing from one bank of a river to the other
The code of conduct that pilgrims follow on the way
A test that traders set for pilgrims

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Pandharpur wari is held every year.
Reason (R): Pilgrims travel to Pandharpur by train in large groups for 21 days.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: the wari is an annual pilgrimage. R is false: the chapter says pilgrims walk in large groups for 21 days.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Explain how the trek to the Sabarimala hilltop shrine is more than just a way of reaching the temple.
questions.a: The shrine was traditionally reached by an immensely difficult trek through hills and forests. The challenging approach symbolises the difficulties of the inner path, and natural landmarks along the route are considered sacred.
s: Describes the difficult trek through hills and forests
States that it symbolises the difficulties of the inner path
Notes that landmarks along the route are sacred

questions.q: Write two questions, each with a one-line answer, that a quiz on the excerpt from Dharampal's travel account could ask.
questions.a: Any two correct pairs, e.g. How long was the pilgrimage? Three months. To which southern place had they gone? Rameswaram. Where were they going next? Haridwar. Why did they not stop in Delhi? They only had to change trains as they had little time.
s: First question is answerable from the excerpt
Second question is different and answerable from the excerpt
Both one-line answers are correct

questions.q: (a) State the age of the Pandharpur wari and the length of the walk. (b) Why is it called a 'wari' and not just a pilgrimage?
questions.a: (a) 800 years old; pilgrims walk for 21 days to the Vithoba temple. (b) Wari means a pilgrimage that is held regularly, in this case annually.
s: Part (a): 800 years and 21 days
Part (b): wari means a regularly held pilgrimage, here annual

questions.q: (a) What does 'tirtha' literally mean? (b) How does the chapter use this meaning to explain why such places are held sacred?
questions.a: (a) A place where one can cross a river or other body of water. (b) Symbolically it becomes a place where one crosses from ordinary worldly life to a higher, spiritual life, so such places are revered.
s: Part (a): literal meaning of crossing a river or water
Part (b): symbolic crossing from worldly to spiritual life as the reason for reverence

questions.q: Differentiate between a 'tirtha' and a 'Tirthankara' as the chapter explains them.
questions.a: A tirtha is a place to cross a river, symbolically to a higher life. A Tirthankara is literally someone who makes a tirtha, that is, guides the crossing from ordinary to higher life; in Jainism the Tirthankaras are the supreme preachers of dharma.
s: Tirtha explained as a crossing place
Tirthankara explained as one who makes a tirtha and guides the crossing

questions.q: Kabir says, 'Long pilgrimages cannot have been made in ancient times because there was no modern transport.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says that for at least 3,000 years, and with no modern means of transportation, Indians have crisscrossed the Subcontinent on pilgrimages, so that its entire geography came to be considered sacred.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Cites at least 3,000 years without modern transport
Adds that the crisscrossing made the whole geography sacred

questions.q: Name three food items the pilgrims in Dharampal's excerpt carried. What does carrying them suggest about how the group travelled?
questions.a: Atta, ghee and sugar. They carried their own food and earthen pots, so they cooked their own meals and were self-reliant on a long journey of about three months.
s: Three items: atta, ghee, sugar
Inference that they cooked for themselves on a long journey

questions.q: The chapter calls a tirthayatra 'not just a physical journey'. What else is it, and what does it require?
questions.a: It is also an inner journey, and it requires a specified code of conduct.
s: Names the inner journey
Names the specified code of conduct

questions.q: 'A tirthayatra is both a physical and an inner journey.' Justify this using the pilgrimage of the group from villages near Lucknow, the Sabarimala trek and the Pandharpur wari.
questions.a: Physical: the group's three-month pilgrimage took in Rameswaram and was ending at Haridwar; Sabarimala involves an immensely difficult trek; the wari is a 21-day walk. Inner: the chapter says pilgrimage requires a specified code of conduct, the Sabarimala trek symbolises the difficulties of the inner path, and a tirtha is a symbolic crossing to a higher life. The tradition has lasted at least 3,000 years.
s: Physical effort in the Lucknow group's journey
Physical effort at Sabarimala and in the wari
Code of conduct as the inner side
Symbolism of the trek or of the tirtha as a crossing
Links both sides to the long tradition

questions.q: Explain the words tirtha and Tirthankara and analyse how the Jain idea of tirtha is connected with the idea of crossing.
questions.a: A tirtha is literally a place to cross a river or water, symbolically a crossing from worldly life to a higher life. A Tirthankara is someone who makes a tirtha by guiding that crossing; Tirthankaras are the supreme preachers of dharma in Jainism. Jain tirthas mark where Tirthankaras attained liberation or where major events of their lives occurred, and trees, ponds, hills and mountains they visited are sacred. Examples are Mount Abu, Girnar and Shatrunjaya.
s: Tirtha explained literally and symbolically
Tirthankara explained as one who makes a tirtha
Jain tirthas linked to liberation and major events
Sacred trees, ponds, hills visited by Tirthankaras
Names an example and ties it back to the crossing idea

questions.q:
In 1961 Jawaharlal Nehru said that pilgrims drawn from the south to the north and from the north to the south showed 'the feeling of one country and one culture'. A traveller on a train met about twelve villagers from two villages north of Lucknow. They said they had spent three months on a pilgrimage up to Rameswaram and were now only changing trains in Delhi for Haridwar. They carried atta, ghee and sugar for food. A shopkeeper at Delhi station suggests they stay one day to buy gifts.
(a) Which term does the chapter use for such a journey, and for each sacred site visited?
(b) What do the food they carried and the months they spent suggest about pilgrimage?
(c) How does the route from Rameswaram to Haridwar support Nehru's words?
(d) Should the group stay a day in Delhi or go straight on? Give a reason from the chapter for your choice.
questions.a: (a) Tirthayatra for the journey and tirtha for each site. (b) That pilgrimage was a long, self-reliant journey needing planning. (c) It runs from the far south to the north, joining distant regions, which suggests a feeling of one country and one culture. (d) Either choice if reasoned: going straight keeps to their purpose and time limit; staying would let them meet traders, and the chapter says pilgrims and traders benefit each other.
s: Part (a): tirthayatra and tirtha
Part (b): long and self-reliant, planned with their own food
Part (c): route links south and north, one country and one culture
Part (d): decision backed by a chapter point on purpose or on pilgrim and trader contact

questions.q:
A Pune school plans a Wari Day on 10 June. The principal offers two options: X, a half-day mock wari in the school ground; Y, a trip to watch the start of the real wari that goes to Pandharpur. Classes resume after the summer break on 24 June. A student says, 'Anyone who starts the real walk on 10 June will be back, or at least at the temple, before classes resume.'
(a) What does the word 'wari' mean?
(b) What does the chapter say about the age and regularity of this wari?
(c) Using the length of the walk given in the chapter and counting 10 June as day one, on which date does the last day of the walk fall? Is the student right?
(d) Choose X or Y and justify it with two points.
questions.a: (a) A pilgrimage held regularly, here every year. (b) It is about 800 years old and held annually, so it is a continuing tradition. (c) The walk lasts 21 days, so day 21 is 30 June, after 24 June: the student is wrong. (d) Either option if reasoned: X lets every student feel a little of the walk without missing school; Y shows the real 800-year-old tradition, but any student who joined the full walk would miss classes.
s: Part (a): wari means a regularly held pilgrimage
Part (b): about 800 years old and annual
Part (c): 30 June, after 24 June, so the student is wrong
Part (d): picks an option and gives two reasons using the earlier answers

questions.q: The Niyam Dongar hill, sacred to the Dongria Khond tribe, lies in which state?
questions.a: Odisha. Tamil Nadu is the state of the Todas, and Sikkim is where sacred sites were identified for protection.
o: Odisha
Tamil Nadu
Sikkim
Meghalaya

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT named as sacred by the Todas of the Nilgiris?
questions.a: Hot springs appear in the list of Sikkim's protected sacred features, not in the Toda list of peaks, plants, Shola forests, wetlands and stones.
o: Hot springs
Shola forests
Wetlands
Specific stones

questions.q: According to the chapter, why is cutting trees on the Niyam Dongar hill prohibited?
questions.a: The Dongria Khond regard the hill as the abode of their supreme deity, Niyam Raja, so cutting trees there is a sign of disrespect.
o: It is seen as disrespect to the deity living on the hill
It is a rule made by the Government of Sikkim
The hill is a relic kept as an object of reverence
The trees are said to be the Tirthankaras' resting places

questions.q: In the chapter, 'Bhudevi' stands for:
questions.a: Mother Earth, the whole planet. The divine mother in the form of Sati and the Dongria Khond deity are different ideas in the chapter.
o: Mother Earth
The supreme deity of the Dongria Khond
The divine mother in the form of Sati
A river honoured as a devi

questions.q: Villagers near a hill tell a company that wants to cut trees there that the hill is the home of their supreme deity, who provides everything they need to live, and that felling trees would insult him. Which community in the chapter holds this belief?
questions.a: This is the Dongria Khond tribe and their Niyam Dongar hill. The Todas, Maoris and Khasi groves appear in the chapter for other beliefs.
o: Dongria Khond of Odisha
Todas of the Nilgiris, who hold many peaks sacred
Maoris of New Zealand, who see a mountain as an ancestor
Khasi people of Meghalaya, who keep khlaw kyntang groves

questions.q:
Consider the statements.
1. In Hinduism, many rivers are regarded as devis.
2. The whole planet Earth is considered sacred as Mother Earth or Bhudevi.
3. Only tribal communities, and never Hindu traditions, treat mountains and trees as sacred.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 is false: the chapter says Hindu belief systems also treat mountains, rivers, forests and trees as sacred. Statements 1 and 2 are stated in the chapter.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Match the community or body in Column A with what the chapter says about it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Dongria Khond  2. Todas  3. Government of Sikkim  4. Hindu belief about the Earth
Column B: a. identified sacred mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs  b. hill that is the abode of Niyam Raja  c. peaks, plants, Shola forests, wetlands and stones are sacred  d. the whole planet is Mother Earth
questions.a: The Dongria Khond - Niyam Dongar; the Todas - peaks, Shola forests and stones; the Sikkim government - the list of protected features; the Hindu view - Mother Earth. Distractors swap the two tribal groups or put the Sikkim list against the Todas.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Cutting trees on the Niyam Dongar hill is prohibited.
Reason (R): The Dongria Khond believe the hill is the abode of Niyam Raja, who provides everything they need for sustenance.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, and the belief in the deity living on the hill is the reason cutting trees is treated as disrespect.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Rhea is writing that a government, and not only a community, can protect sacred places. Which example from the chapter should she use?
questions.a: Sikkim's government identified sacred mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs to be protected from all forms of damage. The other three are community beliefs or practices.
o: Sikkim's listing of its sacred sites for protection
The Dongria Khond ban on cutting trees on the Niyam Dongar hill
The Todas' use of sacred plants in their rituals
The Hindu view of the Earth as Mother Earth, Bhudevi

questions.q: (a) Which community in the Nilgiris regards many mountain peaks as sacred? (b) Besides peaks, name two other things that are sacred to them.
questions.a: (a) The Todas. (b) Any two of plants, Shola forests, wetlands, specific stones, individual trees.
s: Part (a): Todas
Part (b): two correct things

questions.q: Neha says, 'Rivers and mountains are sacred only to tribal communities, not to Hindus.' Test her claim with the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. The chapter says Hindu belief systems also treat specific mountains, rivers and forests as divine and worship them, many rivers are devis, some trees, animals and plants are holy, and the Earth is Bhudevi. Tribal and folk traditions share this view of Nature, so it is not one group alone.
s: Verdict: rejects the claim
Hindu examples of sacred Nature (rivers as devis, trees, Bhudevi)
Notes that folk and tribal traditions share the view, so it is not one group alone

questions.q: Compare the Dongria Khond and the Todas in the way they hold parts of Nature sacred.
questions.a: The Dongria Khond hold the Niyam Dongar hill sacred as the abode of their supreme deity. The Todas hold many peaks sacred and link them with their gods, and extend sacredness to plants used in rituals, Shola forests, wetlands, stones and individual trees. Both treat features of Nature as sacred.
s: Dongria Khond point with the hill and the deity
Todas point with peaks and the wider list
Similarity or contrast stated clearly

questions.q: The picture in the chapter shows Vishnu in the form of a boar saving Bhudevi. Who or what is Bhudevi, and which wider idea does she represent?
questions.a: Bhudevi is Mother Earth; she represents the idea that the whole planet is sacred.
s: Bhudevi named as Mother Earth
Linked to the idea that the whole Earth is sacred

questions.q: The chapter shows Nature held sacred in different parts of India. Name the community and the sacred feature in (a) Odisha and (b) the Nilgiris.
questions.a: (a) The Dongria Khond and the Niyam Dongar hill. (b) The Todas, for example their peaks, plants, Shola forests, wetlands or stones.
s: Part (a): Dongria Khond and Niyam Dongar
Part (b): Todas with a sacred feature

questions.q: (a) Name two things in Nature, other than trees, that the chapter says may be regarded as sacred in Hinduism and folk traditions. (b) What perception, according to the chapter, makes the whole Earth sacred?
questions.a: (a) Any two of particular mountains, rivers, forests, animals or plants. (b) The perception of a divine presence in all of Nature, so the Earth becomes Mother Earth or Bhudevi.
s: Part (a): two correct examples
Part (b): divine presence in all Nature leading to Bhudevi

questions.q: Use Niyam Dongar and Sikkim to explain how a belief that Nature is divine can lead to its protection.
questions.a: At Niyam Dongar the hill is the abode of a deity, so tree cutting is forbidden as disrespect. In Sikkim the government identified sacred mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs to be protected from all forms of damage. In both cases regarding a feature as sacred leads to protection from harm.
s: Niyam Dongar belief and rule
Sikkim identification and protection
Draws the link from sacredness to protection

questions.q: What did the Government of Sikkim do in the early 2000s? Why does this belong in a chapter on sacredness?
questions.a: It identified sacred mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs to be protected from all forms of damage. It shows that sacred natural places were given protection in practice.
s: Describes the identification and protection of sacred features
Links it to the sacredness of Nature

questions.q: 'Ultimately, the whole of planet Earth is considered sacred.' Explain how Hindu, folk and tribal belief systems lead to this idea, using three examples from the chapter.
questions.a: These systems see a divine presence in all of Nature. Mountains, rivers, forests, some trees, animals and plants, and sometimes stones are sacred, and many rivers are devis. Examples: the Niyam Dongar hill of the Dongria Khond, the Toda peaks, plants and Shola forests, and Sikkim's protected sacred places. Since every part of Nature can be divine, the whole planet is Mother Earth or Bhudevi.
s: Divine presence in all of Nature stated as the basis
Hindu examples such as rivers as devis
A tribal example with detail
A second tribal or state example
Conclusion that the whole Earth is Bhudevi

questions.q: Compare the Niyam Dongar hill, the Toda sacred landscape and the Sikkim list of sacred sites, and analyse how both communities and a government can protect the sacred.
questions.a: Niyam Dongar is a hill that is the abode of Niyam Raja, where trees may not be cut. The Todas hold peaks, plants, Shola forests, wetlands and stones sacred. Sikkim's government identified mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs for protection. Communities protect through belief and rules, and a government through identification and protection from all forms of damage.
s: Niyam Dongar described
Toda landscape described
Sikkim list described
Community means of protection analysed
Government means of protection analysed

questions.q:
Pooja is making three revision cards for a display on Nature and the sacred; the headings were lost.
Card 1: 'A hill is the home of a supreme deity; cutting trees there is forbidden.'
Card 2: 'Peaks, plants used in rituals, forests, wetlands, stones and individual trees are sacred.'
Card 3: 'Mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs are listed so that they are protected from all forms of damage.'
(a) Which community and place belong on Card 1, which community on Card 2, and which state on Card 3?
(b) Which card describes protection by a government rather than a community's belief?
(c) Card 2 lists six kinds of natural feature and Card 3 lists five. If mountains and peaks count as one kind, how many different kinds are on the two cards together?
(d) A friend says, 'Cards 1 and 3 prove sacred places are protected only by laws made by governments.' Decide whether this is right, using the cards.
questions.a: (a) Card 1: the Dongria Khond and the Niyam Dongar hill; Card 2: the Todas; Card 3: Sikkim. (b) Card 3. (c) 6 + 5 - 1 = 10 kinds. (d) The friend is wrong: Card 1 shows a community's belief produces a rule against cutting trees, with no law needed, while Card 3 shows a government protecting sacred features; so protection comes from both beliefs and governments.
s: Part (a): Dongria Khond with Niyam Dongar, Todas, Sikkim
Part (b): Card 3 as the government's action
Part (c): 10 kinds
Part (d): rejects 'only' using Card 1 as a counter-example

questions.q:
Aarav's class from Coimbatore is going to the Nilgiris. The guide tells them that the local Todas regard many mountain peaks as sacred. The teacher plans two activities: (X) collecting a few plant samples for a school herbarium, only after the elders give permission; (Y) sketching the landscape and interviewing an elder.
(a) Name the type of forest and two other natural things, apart from peaks, that the Todas hold sacred.
(b) Why might collecting plants be sensitive here even if permission is asked?
(c) What does the Toda view add to the chapter's idea that Nature is sacred?
(d) Which activity would you choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) Shola forests; any two of plants, wetlands, specific stones, individual trees. (b) Plants often become part of Toda rituals, so removing them could disrespect what is sacred. (c) It shows that sacredness can extend over a whole landscape, not only a single shrine. (d) Either if reasoned: X is acceptable because the elders' permission and a small collection respect the community; Y takes nothing from the place and learns directly from an elder.
s: Part (a): Shola forests plus two other sacred things
Part (b): plants used in rituals make collection sensitive
Part (c): sacredness spreads over a landscape
Part (d): choice justified with a chapter point

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT correct about the 12 jyotirlingas?
questions.a: They are dedicated to Shiva, not Vishnu. The other three statements are made in the chapter.
o: They are shrines dedicated to Vishnu
Each has its own unique mythology and name
They are considered highly auspicious
They form a network that spreads across India

questions.q: The chapter says the four char dham sites appear to have been deliberately placed in:
questions.a: The southern, northern, eastern and western corners of India. The four Kumbh places are a different set of four.
o: The four corners of India
The four places where drops of amrita fell
The four Sikh takht towns
The four banks of the Prayag sangam

questions.q: How many Shakti pithas does the chapter say cover the map of India?
questions.a: 51. The number 12 belongs to the jyotirlingas and 19 to the rivers in the nadistuti sukta.

questions.q: According to the story in the chapter, the Shakti pithas are the places where:
questions.a: The body parts of Sati fell one by one after Vishnu used his chakra to cut up her body. Nectar fell at the Kumbh places.
o: Parts of the divine mother's body fell
Drops of amrita fell from the pitcher
Tirthankaras attained liberation
The Buddha's relics are kept

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. The 12 jyotirlingas are shrines dedicated to Shiva.
2. Pilgrims on these networks met diverse languages, foods and customs but also noticed commonalities.
3. Debates, trade and the sharing of tales along the routes became a major factor in the cultural integration of the Subcontinent.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three are stated in the chapter. The jyotirlingas honour Shiva, pilgrims noticed both differences and commonalities, and the exchanges helped integration.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: A cloth merchant from Madurai, a teacher going to debate and a pilgrim all take the same road to Varanasi. What, according to the chapter, was the likely result of such meetings?
questions.a: Exchange of goods, experiences and ideas, which became a major factor in cultural integration. The routes converged because the journeys overlapped.
o: Exchange of goods and ideas, aiding cultural integration
The routes separated so that each group kept to its own region
Pilgrimage turned into a purely commercial activity carried on by merchants
Local languages were replaced by a single common language

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Shakti pithas lie across India and also in parts of present-day Bangladesh and Pakistan.
Reason (R): The Shakti pithas are the places where drops of amrita fell from the pitcher.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: the 51 Shakti pithas cover the map of India and extend into these countries. R is false: the places where Sati's body parts fell are the pithas; the drops of amrita fell at the Kumbh places.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Rohan sees that the four char dham sites lie in four different corners of India. What might this have meant for pilgrims who wished to visit all four?
questions.a: Because the sites appear to be deliberately located in the four corners, visiting all four means travelling north-south and east-west across the country. This is an inference; the book only says the placement appears deliberate.
o: They would have had to travel across the whole of the country
They would have had to visit only the northern mountains
They would have found all four beside the Kumbh rivers
They would have avoided every trade route

questions.q: The chapter says that networks of tirthas 'crisscross India's length and breadth, creating a sacred geography'. What is the result for the land itself?
questions.a: The land itself becomes sacred, because the sacred places are spread across and linked over the whole country.
s: States that the land itself becomes sacred
Connects this to the spread and linking of the networks

questions.q: Give three reasons, from the chapter, why people travelled long distances on the routes to sacred places.
questions.a: Religious motives; merchants and traders travelled to exchange goods; some travelled to discuss, debate and popularise beliefs; others went to learn from eminent teachers in different parts of the country.
s: Names one reason correctly
Names a second different reason
Names a third different reason

questions.q: Briefly tell the story the chapter gives about the 51 Shakti pithas, naming who cut up Sati's body and with what.
questions.a: Sati, the divine mother, immolated herself after her father insulted her and Shiva. Shiva took her body and refused the last rites, which endangered the world, so Vishnu used his chakra to cut her body; the places where the parts fell are the Shakti pithas.
s: Shiva's grief and anger over Sati
Vishnu's chakra and the falling of the parts at the pithas

questions.q: What is meant by 'sacred geography'? Give one network from the chapter as an example.
questions.a: A pattern in which networks of sacred places spread across a land make the land itself sacred. Example: the char dham, the 12 jyotirlingas or the 51 Shakti pithas.
s: Explains sacred geography as networks making the land sacred
Gives a correct network

questions.q: Show that the four char dham sites cannot all lie in the north of India, using what the chapter says about their positions.
questions.a: The chapter says the sites appear to be deliberately located in the southern, northern, eastern and western corners of India. Four corners mean one site in each direction, so at most one is in the north.
s: Quotes the four-corner placement
Reasons that this puts one site in each direction
Concludes that only one can be in the north

questions.q: (a) Name two kinds of travellers, other than pilgrims, who used the same routes. (b) How did their meetings contribute to cultural integration?
questions.a: (a) Any two of merchants and traders, teachers, debaters or learners. (b) Their routes converged and discussions, sharing of goods, experiences and tales enriched everyone, with new ideas emerging and old ones adapted.
s: Part (a): two correct types of travellers
Part (b): converging routes and exchange of ideas and goods

questions.q: Dev says, 'On a pilgrimage along these networks, travellers would find everything unfamiliar and nothing in common.' Test his claim with the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Pilgrims met diverse languages, customs, clothing and foods, but the chapter says they would notice the commonalities too, which helped build cultural integration.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong, not half right
Admits the diversity found
Adds the commonalities noticed

questions.q: (a) Whose shrines are the 12 jyotirlingas? (b) The Shakti pithas lie across India and even parts of present-day Bangladesh and Pakistan. What does the story behind them symbolise?
questions.a: (a) Shiva's. (b) That the whole land becomes the body of the divine mother.
s: Part (a): Shiva
Part (b): the whole land as the body of the divine mother

questions.q: Explain how pilgrimage and the travel linked with it helped the cultural integration of the Indian Subcontinent.
questions.a: Pilgrims visiting major sacred places covered the geography of India and met diverse languages, customs, clothing and foods, but noticed commonalities too. Merchants, traders, debaters and students travelled the same routes, which converged. Discussions, debates and sharing of goods, experiences and tales enriched everyone, new ideas emerged and old ones were adapted. This was a major factor in cultural integration.
s: Pilgrims cover the geography of India
Meeting diversity and noticing commonalities
Other travellers on converging routes
Exchange of goods, tales and ideas
Concludes that this helped cultural integration

questions.q: 'Networks of tirthas crisscross India, creating a sacred geography.' Justify this with the char dham, the jyotirlingas and the Shakti pithas, and explain the symbol in the Shakti pitha story.
questions.a: The char dham lie in the four corners of India. The 12 jyotirlingas are Shiva shrines linked as one set. The 51 Shakti pithas cover the entire map, even parts of present-day Bangladesh and Pakistan. In the story Sati's body was cut up by Vishnu with his chakra and the parts fell across the land, symbolising that the whole land is the body of the divine mother.
s: Char dham spread in four corners
Jyotirlingas as a network of 12 Shiva shrines
Shakti pithas covering the map
The story of Sati's body falling
Symbol: the whole land as the divine mother's body

questions.q:
Anita's class in Hyderabad is making a wall chart called 'One land, many shrines'. They have room for just one network: the char dham, the jyotirlingas or the Shakti pithas. Their teacher says that one of these networks reaches into countries beyond present-day India, and that its shared story carries a symbol about the land itself.
(a) How many sites are there in each of the three networks?
(b) Which network reaches beyond present-day India, and into which two countries?
(c) What symbol does the story behind that network carry?
(d) Which network would you choose for the chart, and why?
questions.a: (a) Char dham: four; jyotirlingas: 12; Shakti pithas: 51. (b) The Shakti pithas; parts of present-day Bangladesh and Pakistan. (c) The whole land becomes the body of the divine mother. (d) Either network if justified: the Shakti pithas for their spread and symbol of the whole land; the char dham for showing the four corners clearly.
s: Part (a): four, 12 and 51
Part (b): Shakti pithas, Bangladesh and Pakistan
Part (c): whole land as the divine mother's body
Part (d): choice supported by a chapter point

questions.q:
Three people set out together from Madurai for Varanasi on an old route: Kumar with bales of cloth, Gayatri with palm-leaf manuscripts she hopes to discuss with scholars, and Meera, who is making a pilgrimage. At night in the inns they hear many languages, taste unfamiliar foods and share stories. A local council on the route will build one rest house. Beside the famous shrine, a night count shows 90 pilgrims, 30 merchants and 20 teachers or students. Beside the busy market it shows 20 pilgrims, 100 merchants and 5 teachers or students.
(a) Give the reason for travel that applies to each of Kumar and Gayatri.
(b) Which site has more travellers on a night, and by how many?
(c) What larger effect did such shared journeys have on the Subcontinent?
(d) Where should the council build the rest house? Justify using the chapter and the counts.
questions.a: (a) Kumar: to exchange goods as a merchant; Gayatri: to discuss and debate and learn from others. (b) Shrine: 90 + 30 + 20 = 140; market: 20 + 100 + 5 = 125; the shrine has 15 more. (c) Cultural integration, through exchange of goods, experiences, tales and ideas. (d) Either if reasoned: the shrine has more travellers and more teachers and pilgrims meeting merchants, so more exchange of ideas; the market has mostly merchants, so goods change hands but fewer ideas and tales mix.
s: Part (a): trade for Kumar, discussion and debate for Gayatri
Part (b): shrine 140, market 125, shrine by 15
Part (c): cultural integration
Part (d): site chosen using the counts and the chapter's idea of exchange along converging routes

questions.q: In the legend of amrita manthana, who snatched the pitcher of amrita to keep it from the asuras?
questions.a: Vishnu, in the form of Mohini, a beautiful lady. The boar form belongs to the image of rescuing Bhudevi.
o: Vishnu in the form of Mohini
Vishnu in the form of a boar
Shiva carrying Sati's body
The devas' king in his own form

questions.q: At which place do the Ganga, the Yamuna and the invisible Sarasvati meet?
questions.a: Prayag (Prayagraj). Haridwar, Nashik and Ujjain are the other Kumbh places but are not this sangam.
o: Prayag
Haridwar
Nashik
Ujjain

questions.q: The nadistuti sukta of the Rigveda is a hymn in praise of how many major rivers of ancient northwest India?
questions.a: 19. The verse used in water rituals today names seven rivers, which is a different count.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four places where, in the legend, drops of amrita fell?
questions.a: Varanasi is a sacred city mentioned elsewhere but is not one of the four Kumbh places: Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain.
o: Varanasi
Haridwar
Nashik
Ujjain

questions.q:
Study the statements.
1. Only the Ganga is addressed with respect as 'ji'; other rivers are never addressed so.
2. A dip in the rivers at the Kumbh places is considered auspicious at any time of the year.
3. The Kumbh Mela originates in the legend of amrita manthana.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: the chapter also gives 'Yamuna ji'. 2 is false: the dip is auspicious during a prescribed period. 3 is stated in the chapter.
o: 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q: At a school fair a poster says, 'The Kumbh Mela is a stone monument that UNESCO protects.' Karan wants to correct it using the chapter. What should he write instead?
questions.a: The chapter says UNESCO listed the Kumbh Mela as an intangible heritage of the world, a living practice and not a building.
o: UNESCO has listed it as an intangible heritage of the world
UNESCO has listed it as a world heritage monument at Prayagraj
UNESCO has named it a natural wonder of the Ganga
UNESCO has listed it as one of the 19 rivers of the Rigveda

questions.q:
Assertion (A): UNESCO listed the Kumbh Mela as an intangible heritage of the world.
Reason (R): An estimated 660 million people participated in the Kumbh Mela of 2025.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but the listing was made a few years before 2025, so the 2025 attendance cannot be its explanation.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match the term in Column A with the correct description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Nadistuti sukta  2. Prayag  3. Amrita manthana  4. 'Ganga ji'
Column B: a. a way rivers are addressed with respect  b. hymn in praise of 19 rivers  c. meeting point of three rivers  d. legend behind the Kumbh Mela
questions.a: The hymn praises 19 rivers, Prayag is the sangam, the churning legend explains the Kumbh and 'ji' is a respectful form of address. The distractors swap the hymn with the legend or the sangam with the form of address.

questions.q: During a ritual, Asha hears the priest recite 'Ganga, Yamuna, Godavari, Sarasvati, Narmada, Sindhu and Kaveri, may you manifest in this water.' What does the chapter say this shows?
questions.a: Many rituals involving water invoke the presence of some of the most important rivers of India. It does not limit sacred rivers to seven.
o: Rituals invoke some of India's main rivers
Only these seven rivers are sacred anywhere in India
The Rigveda hymn names just these seven great rivers
Rivers can be worshipped only at a sangam of rivers

questions.q: (a) What is the nadistuti sukta? (b) Name any four rivers from the verse that is recited in water rituals today.
questions.a: (a) A hymn of the Rigveda in praise of rivers that invokes 19 major rivers of ancient northwest India. (b) Any four of Ganga, Yamuna, Godavari, Sarasvati, Narmada, Sindhu, Kaveri.
s: Part (a): hymn in praise of 19 rivers of the northwest
Part (b): four rivers correctly named

questions.q: Describe in two or three sentences how the legend of amrita manthana explains where the Kumbh Mela is held.
questions.a: Devas and asuras churned the cosmic ocean to get amrita; Vishnu as Mohini snatched the pitcher (kumbha), and in the process a few drops fell at Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain, where the Kumbh Mela is held.
s: Churning and the pitcher of amrita
Drops falling at the four places where the Mela is held

questions.q: Rahul says, 'The verse recited in rituals names seven rivers, so the Rigveda praises just seven rivers.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. The nadistuti sukta of the Rigveda invokes 19 major rivers of ancient northwest India. The seven-river verse is one that is used in water rituals even today, so he confuses the two.
s: Verdict: not right
Gives 19 rivers for the nadistuti sukta
Separates it from the seven-river ritual verse

questions.q: (a) What is a sangam? (b) Name the three rivers at Prayag and say which one is described as invisible.
questions.a: (a) The confluence of rivers. (b) Ganga, Yamuna and Sarasvati; the Sarasvati is invisible.
s: Part (a): sangam as a confluence of rivers
Part (b): the three rivers and the invisible Sarasvati

questions.q: Why does the chapter call rivers 'lifelines for the Indian civilisation'? Mention how people speak of them in local languages.
questions.a: Rivers have sustained the civilisation, and their sources, tributaries and the places they flow through are regarded as sacred and visited by pilgrims. In local languages they are addressed with respect, as 'Ganga ji' or 'Yamuna ji'.
s: Rivers as lifelines whose sources and banks are sacred
Respectful address such as Ganga ji

questions.q: How often does Prayagraj host the Kumbh Mela according to the chapter, and what is considered most auspicious at the Kumbh places?
questions.a: Every six years; a dip in the rivers there during a prescribed period.
s: Every six years
A dip in the rivers during a prescribed period

questions.q: Use the legend to show that the Kumbh Mela cannot be held at one place only.
questions.a: In the legend a few drops of amrita fell over four places, Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain. These are the places where the Kumbh Mela has been held, so it cannot belong to one place alone.
s: States the drops fell at four places
Names the four places
Concludes the Mela is held at all of them, not one

questions.q: Why are the sources, tributaries and banks of rivers often visited by pilgrims? Give three points from the chapter.
questions.a: Rivers are lifelines of the civilisation; their sources, tributaries and the places they flow through are regarded as sacred; tirthas are usually on the banks of a river or lake; rituals invoke rivers and they are addressed with respect.
s: Rivers as lifelines
Sources, tributaries and places along them regarded as sacred
Tirthas located on banks or rituals invoking rivers

questions.q: 'In India rivers are not just water.' Justify this statement using the nadistuti sukta, the water-ritual verse, the way rivers are addressed, and the location of tirthas.
questions.a: Rivers have been worshipped since Vedic times; the nadistuti sukta praises 19 major rivers. Rituals today invoke Ganga, Yamuna, Godavari, Sarasvati, Narmada, Sindhu and Kaveri in the water. They are addressed with respect as Ganga ji or Yamuna ji. Tirthas are usually on the banks of rivers or lakes, and the sources and tributaries are visited too. They are lifelines of the civilisation.
s: Worship since Vedic times and the nadistuti sukta
The ritual verse invoking rivers
Respectful forms of address
Tirthas and sources on riverbanks
Rivers as lifelines linking the earlier points

questions.q: Describe the legend behind the Kumbh Mela and use its scale and its UNESCO listing to explain why it is described as a heritage of the world.
questions.a: Devas and asuras churned the cosmic ocean for amrita; Vishnu as Mohini snatched the pitcher and drops fell at Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain. A dip in the rivers during a prescribed period is auspicious. Prayagraj, at the sangam of Ganga, Yamuna and the invisible Sarasvati, hosts it every six years. About 660 million people took part in 2025 and UNESCO listed it as an intangible heritage of the world, which is why it is called a heritage of the world.
s: Churning and the pitcher
Four places where drops fell
Dip in rivers and the sangam at Prayagraj
Scale: about 660 million in 2025
UNESCO listing as intangible heritage of the world linked to the description

questions.q:
Ria's Class 7 of 40 students is preparing a project on the Kumbh Mela. The teacher says that, at the interval the chapter gives, Prayagraj hosted the Mela in 2025. The group can plan a visit either to the next Mela at Prayagraj, costing Rs 1,800 per student, or to the river bank in their own town at a quiet time, costing nothing. The project fund is Rs 60,000.
(a) Name the other three places where the Mela is held.
(b) In which year will Prayagraj next host the Mela at this interval, and by how much would the Prayagraj visit exceed the fund?
(c) What has UNESCO done for the Kumbh Mela?
(d) Which plan would you recommend for Class 7, and why?
questions.a: (a) Haridwar, Nashik and Ujjain. (b) 2031 (2025 + 6); 40 x 1,800 = Rs 72,000, which is Rs 12,000 more than the fund. (c) Listed it as an intangible heritage of the world. (d) Either if reasoned: the Mela offers a living view of the legend and the sangam but needs Rs 12,000 more; the local riverbank fits the fund and allows a calmer study of how rivers are respected.
s: Part (a): Haridwar, Nashik and Ujjain
Part (b): 2031 and Rs 12,000 over the fund
Part (c): intangible heritage listing
Part (d): plan chosen with the cost and a chapter point

questions.q:
In the town of Nashik, a ritual begins with a verse that invokes seven major rivers to be present in the water. The Godavari ghat in the town has tirthas on its bank and many pilgrims bathe there. The town committee has Rs 3,00,000 and two proposals: new lighting for the ghat at Rs 1,40,000 and a riverbank clean-up at Rs 1,90,000.
(a) Name any four of the rivers the verse invokes and say what it asks of them.
(b) Can the committee fund both proposals? Show the amount by which it is short or has left over.
(c) Why does the chapter say rivers deserve respect, and how are they addressed in local languages?
(d) Which proposal should be done first, and why?
questions.a: (a) Any four of Ganga, Yamuna, Godavari, Sarasvati, Narmada, Sindhu, Kaveri; it asks them to manifest (be present) in the water. (b) No: 1,40,000 + 1,90,000 = 3,30,000, which is Rs 30,000 more than the Rs 3,00,000 available. (c) They are lifelines of the civilisation; addressed as Ganga ji, Yamuna ji. (d) Either if reasoned: clean-up protects the river and the tirthas on its banks that pilgrims value; lighting helps pilgrims who come in numbers to the ghat.
s: Part (a): four rivers named and the request that they be present in the water
Part (b): total 3,30,000, short by Rs 30,000
Part (c): lifelines, addressed with respect as ji
Part (d): priority chosen with a chapter-based reason

questions.q: Why does the chapter say many tirthas and temples are located on hilltops?
questions.a: Mountains are seen as a symbolic gateway from earth to heaven because of their height, so the climb becomes a symbolic journey to reach the divine.
o: Mountains are seen as a symbolic gateway from earth to heaven
Hilltops were the only places where rivers could be crossed
Traders had fixed their markets on the hilltops
Sacred groves can grow only on hills

questions.q:
A village in Kerala has 480 families and a sacred grove. A company offers to buy the grove land for a factory and promises one job for every 8 families, and to build a school for the village. The panchayat will decide at the next gram sabha.
(a) What is a sacred grove called in Malayalam?
(b) How many families would get a job under the company's promise, and how many would not?
(c) Name two things the chapter says such groves give to their surroundings.
(d) Should the panchayat accept the offer? Give a reasoned recommendation.
questions.a: (a) Kavu. (b) 480 / 8 = 60 families get a job; 480 - 60 = 420 do not. (c) Any two of shelter for great biodiversity, small water bodies that help water conservation, protection of the forest from hunting, felling and mining. (d) Either decision if reasoned: accepting gives 60 jobs and a school but loses a grove that shelters biodiversity and water and that the chapter says is shrinking; refusing keeps these but gives up the jobs and school, so the panchayat could bargain for the school without selling the grove.
s: Part (a): kavu
Part (b): 60 families with jobs and 420 without
Part (c): two benefits of groves from the chapter
Part (d): recommendation using the numbers and a chapter point

questions.q:
Meera's teacher shows a seal from Mohenjo-daro with leaves at the top that look like those of a peepul, and says the tree at the Mahabodhi Temple in Bodh Gaya is cited as a descendant of the tree under which, in Buddhist tradition, the Buddha attained enlightenment. The town municipality plans to cut an old peepul beside the school road to widen it, because school buses and ambulances jam there. Widening by cutting the tree costs Rs 6,00,000; widening around the tree, by moving the compound wall and bus stop, costs Rs 7,50,000.
(a) What does the seal suggest about the peepul in India's culture?
(b) Give the botanical name of the peepul and the four faiths to which it is sacred.
(c) How much more does it cost to widen the road around the tree, and what two benefits of the tree does the chapter mention?
(d) Should the road be widened by cutting the tree, or planned around it? Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) That the peepul has been part of India's cultural geography for millennia. (b) Ficus religiosa; Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism and Jainism. (c) Rs 1,50,000 more; any two of leaves for skin ailments, bark for stomach ailments, food and shelter for birds and other animals. (d) Either if reasoned: planning around it costs Rs 1,50,000 more but keeps a tree sacred to four faiths and useful to people and birds; cutting is cheaper and clears the jam sooner but loses all of these.
s: Part (a): an important part of India's cultural geography for millennia
Part (b): Ficus religiosa and the four faiths
Part (c): Rs 1,50,000 more and two benefits of the tree
Part (d): decision justified with the cost and chapter points
